Common questions

Plain answers for patients and families. Your own care team knows your situation best.

I was just diagnosed. What should I do first?
Ask your care team three things: the exact type of cancer, its stage, and the goal of treatment — cure, control or comfort. Bring a friend or family member, write your questions down, and ask for copies of your reports. The visit guide has a printable list of questions.
How do I look up a medicine my doctor mentioned?
Type the brand or generic name in the search box at the top of this page — for example Rituxan or rituximab — or browse Cancer medicines A to Z. The name on your pharmacy label or treatment calendar works too.
What is the difference between chemotherapy, immunotherapy and targeted therapy?
Chemotherapy damages fast-growing cells. Immunotherapy helps your own immune system attack the cancer. Targeted therapy blocks a specific signal the cancer uses to grow. Many treatment plans combine them. More in plain words.
When should I call my care team right away?
Call right away for a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, shaking chills, trouble breathing, chest pain, bleeding that won’t stop, vomiting or diarrhea that won’t stop, or new confusion. During treatment a fever can be an emergency even if you feel fine. For a medical emergency, call 911.
Will I lose my hair?
It depends on the medicine. Many treatments — including most immunotherapy, targeted therapy and hormone therapy — usually do not cause full hair loss. Some chemotherapy does. Ask your team about your plan, and whether a scalp-cooling cap is an option.
Can I take vitamins, herbs or supplements?
Tell your care team about everything you take, including teas, herbs, vitamins and remedies from home or from another country. Some can weaken treatment or increase side effects. Bring the bottles to your visit.
What does my scan or biopsy report mean?
Reports are written for doctors and can be confusing or frightening to read alone. Write down the words you don’t understand and go over them with your oncologist. What PET, CT and MRI can and can’t show.
Is palliative care the same as hospice?
No. Palliative care is extra support for pain and symptoms at any stage, even alongside treatment meant to cure. Hospice is comfort-focused care when treatment is no longer helping. Learn about palliative care.
Should I ask about clinical trials?
Yes. A clinical trial may offer a newer treatment with close follow-up. Ask your oncologist whether one fits your cancer and stage. You can also search ClinicalTrials.gov.
Is my cancer inherited?
Most cancers are not inherited, but some run in families. If close relatives had cancer — especially at a young age — ask about genetic counseling and testing. Look up a gene.

About Dr. Ehsan

Dr. Alex Ehsan is a medical oncologist, hematologist and internist who cares for adults with cancer and blood disorders across Los Angeles, and supports patients and families through palliative and hospice care.

He started this free website because patients kept asking the same good questions — and deserved clear, written answers they could take home and share.
